chunks: "A solenoid moves in a few milliseconds over a few millimetres, so I think in terms of transit time and short-range linear sensors rather than rpm.
The simplest way is timing: put two sensors a known distance apart along the stroke, say optical gates or Hall sensors, and time the plunger between them.
Velocity is the distance over the time, and a microcontroller timer gives microsecond resolution.
For average velocity I only need start and end of the stroke: stroke length over transit time, so a 10 mm stroke in 8 milliseconds is about 1. 25 m/s.
If I have a continuous position sensor, like a linear Hall sensor with a magnet on the plunger or an LVDT, I can differentiate it, but I'd filter because differentiation amplifies noise.
And if I don't want any sensor, the coil itself works. The coil equation has a term, current times dL/dx times velocity, which is the motional back-EMF.
When the plunger accelerates, it pulls current down, so under constant voltage drive you see the current rise, dip and rise again.
The depth and timing of the dip are tied to velocity and the arrival time. That's the same idea as measuring motor speed from back-EMF.
In the lab I'd confirm with a high-speed camera or a laser displacement sensor."
